sections.h:
She hears she is now at Sampierdarena. She is to see how the community is going and step in with suitable advice and decisions. She thinks the postulancy could work well at Sampierdarena. She is greatly grieved about Gigino and begs her to look after him. She suggests some Sisters for the new community.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received your letter an hour ago.1 I hear you have arrived at S. P. d'Arena: blessed be God! I'll answer everything you say. First, help the Sister Superior as much as you can; indeed I'll give you various instructions about this, with the greatest prudence. Listen: keep an eye on Sr. A. Angiola and all her ways, and then on all the others, because they complain strongly that the Superior is too strict.2

2. I think it's because they dislike being subject; anyway, see for yourself how things are going and then suggest to the Superior how she should act. And in my name too I tell you to scold and give orders as you think fit.

3. I've written to Don Accinelli that the postulancy should be kept at S. P. d'Arena. See what you think; I believe it would be good to do so.3

4. I can't wait for you to write me something about the hospital.

5. Now something else: I ask you (to do) to find out how Gigino is, what he does, what he says, how he is, where he sleeps, where he eats. How my heart aches! I cannot hide my extreme grief. Poor boy! Alone, left to himself. Alas, my Francesca, what sorrow it is for me! Ah, for pity's sake, see whether the Daughters of Saint Anne in Genoa can give him his meals, and I

will pay them something for his board; speak to Don Accinelli about it, let him hear these lines; as for lodging, I hope he will stay with that angel Don Accinelli.4

6. I would also need to have him here, for certain things only a friend can know, and to have his advice; you can imagine. Yesterday I had the Holy Father's audience, which comforted me, but it's not enough; I cannot write.5

7. I think Piacenza could easily send you the cook. You can take Sr. A. Elisabetta from Nizza with Sr. A. Luigia; what do you say? It would work: put Sr. A. Elisabetta in charge of the wardrobe, and Sr. A. — the one you take from Genoa — as portress and so on; as cook, the one in Piacenza; Sr. A. Luigia stays as nurse. There, all well arranged. Or you can take one from the S. P. d'Arena house, (a) Giacinta; she can serve instead of Sr. A. Luigia, and then you'd take only Sr. A. Elisabetta from Nizza; what do you think? If you see others would suit you better, go ahead, for this is only my advice, not an order.6

8. So try to make a contract with the hospital. Listen: I've written to the Mayor that I'll see to the Chapel apart from the sacred vessels; you can tell him so too. For Poss I've found everything and am sending it all to Piacenza: chalice, pyx, chasubles; I still lack the humeral veil; I'm making one consignment.

Goodbye. Give my regards to the Superior Augusta and encourage her

your affectionate M. ROSA

1 your letter: dated 30.1.74.

2 The Sister Superior of the Sampierdarena house: Sr. A. Augusta Biagini.

keep an eye... Sr. A. Angiola Degrossi. From her and the other Sisters complaints

had reached her about the Superior.

3 Don Accinelli: cf. L 2, n. 4; postulancy: L 183,4.

4 how Gigino is... my heart aches. Expressions full of love and

sorrow; they are a cry from the soul of this mother, of whom God asks what he has asked of

very few, reserving her life entirely to himself alone and to his Kingdom.

5 To have him here: she means Accinelli, a true and trusted friend. Audience with the

Holy Father: cf. L 186,2.

6 A moment of discernment: she suggests some Sisters who could

form the community for the new Sampierdarena hospital, but only as

advice. Her Francesca has the experience and judgement to choose whom she wants. Sr. A.

Elisabetta Veronesi and Sr. A. Luigia were at Nizza Monferrato; Sr. A. Giacinta Anto-

niazzi at Sampierdarena.

7 ...apart from the oratura: i.e. the sacred vessels (chalices, pyxes, etc.).

In the previous letter she told her to look after the Sampierdarena house, among other news. She wants to know when she will go to Piacenza and gives her some errands to see to there; she then awaits reports.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. I've just finished reading your letter. I note what you say. I hope you have received my other one and will see that I already told you to look after this house and assigned the Sisters you were to take with you to the hospital; now I tell you to do all you say regarding the confessor, and anything else you think right; as for the contract, you did well to answer as you did.1

2. I'd like to know what day you'll return to Piacenza, so you can do what I am now writing. Send for Sr. A. Sofia at Cortemaggiore and send another there instead; for sewing anyone will do, even Sr. A. Giovanna, as long as she does no harm with her tongue; better choose another, but for charity's sake make sure she is good.2

3. You can tell the Mayor you are going to fetch the others and the other things; you can have the pigs slaughtered and do what you left undone.3

4. Listen, back to Sr. A. Sofia: send her here with Sr. A. Ignazia from Ferrara; register the letter when you write to Ferrara to arrange for the Sisters to meet; forbid Sr. A. Sofia, for charity's sake, to visit anyone in Bologna. You'll order her, won't you?4

5. Horror! S.C... is a villain of the first order; what a business,

my dear! Enough, I'm afraid to write like this; I'll go no further.5 Write me something about Alessandro, for I am very, very anxious; you can't imagine.6

6. When you decide to leave — and I'd like it to be soon, so you can send me Sr. A. Sofia — tell me how you found things, whether it can work or not with Poss. I wrote to him that I absolutely cannot agree to his requests; it is impossible; for your guidance.7

7. As for your nose, which you mention, it must be overheating; don't overtax yourself and cool down, for charity's sake.

8. Tell me how long mamma will stay at Pegli and why they closed the house and didn't take Alessandro with them. Tell me lots of things, for I long to hear, being so anxious.8

Goodbye. I am your

affectionate M. R.

9. Don't let anyone notice that I write to you and call you 'tu', because

I no longer do so with anyone. Goodbye, dear daughter; look after yourself, for

pity's sake.9

Give my regards to Don Accinelli.

1 My other one: L 187. Regarding the confessor. This concerns the Sam-

pierdarena house: the confessor had made some remarks to the Superior Augusta, and

Sr. A. Francesca had advised her how to reply. On the contract with the hospital

administration, Sr. A. Francesca had expressed the Institute's

willingness. (Cf. letters of Camisa to M. Rosa 1.2.74 and Accinelli to M. Rosa 3.2.74).

2 Sr. A. Sofia Pasti could be replaced as wardrobe keeper by Sr. A. Giovanna Bixio or

another Sister.

3 The pigs: there was the problem of having them slaughtered, and Don Accinelli had not

yet found the right man. Cf. L 182, n. 6.

4 Sr. A. Sofia Pasti was to leave for Rome. In Bologna she would meet

Sr. A. Ignazia Losi coming from Ferrara. Sr. A. Sofia was not to stop in Bologna

for any reason. This Sister was a native of Bologna.

5 S.C. is Sr. A. del S. Cuore Cocchella, superior of the "Casa delle Serve"

in Trastevere. Cf. L 189, n. 1 and 194, n. 13.

6 Cf. L 187,5.

7 Tell me how things are going regarding the Poss factory.

8 After Mr Francesco Gattorno's death, Mrs Adelaide had gone

with Mrs Giustina and family to Pegli. (Letter of Camisa to M. Rosa 30.1.1874). Ales-

sandro was with them too.

9 Cf. L 133,2.

She tells her to send Sr. A. Sofia with the utmost urgency, as she needs her; to encourage the Superior and to act with courage and without human respect.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. My Francesca, listen: my head is a thousand miles away; I'm afraid my brain will turn to water; for charity's sake, see that Sr. A. Sofia comes at once; I need her desperately. When you hear why, you'll clutch your head and exclaim: my God! is it possible! is it possible!1

2. Silence, that ne[...], and send her to me at once, at once, with Ignazia. Give Sr. A. Augusta this note; encourage her, and at the same time don't fail to act courageously, firmly, without human respect.2

3. As soon as I can I'll write to Don Accinelli. Meanwhile he will receive my other power of attorney tomorrow. Patience! All matters are going well; God helped us; my dear, if they find any brain left in me when I die, it will be a miracle.3

Goodbye, yours for ever

M. R.

4. P.S. For charity's sake, don't encourage his attitude of being above

everyone. You see, my dear, having money he goes to the inn, and that

isn't right; if he has nothing he'll be humbler.4

1 Something serious had certainly happened at the Trastevere House in

Rome, making it necessary to replace the Superior Sr. A. del Cuore Cocchella urgently.

2 che ne e: silence about this. With Ignazia, cf. L 188,4; give...

respect, cf. L 187,1-2.

3 She had appointed Don Antonio Accinelli her attorney so that, her father

having died, he might protect her interests regarding the inheritance. She had had to redo

the document because of an error that made it invalid; cf. letter of Accinelli 3.2.74.

4 She means Alessandro. Don't encourage his proud character; when he has

money, he plays the great man.

She is pleased with how she is acting. She is to go ahead without human respect, doing everything for God's glory. She explains the various moves of Sisters to form the new community and urges her to go to Piacenza to send off two Sisters and see to the girls working at the Poss factory.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I have just received yours and am glad to hear of the order you are bringing into that unfortunate house. Courage, without human respect; forward, my dear, without fear of being well or ill regarded; all for the glory of God and nothing else.1

2. I hope you've received my letter telling you to send Sr. A. Sofia at once with Ignazia; I also tell you not to take Sr. A. Elvira at all for now, because it would be a mistake; so I hope you'll take the ones I wrote to you about.2

3. As cook, the one in Piacenza we mentioned seems very good to me. You could take Pacifica and send another to Ovada, but you'll see that the one in Piacenza still needs a little time, and then she'll be much better. So you are four: Sr. A. from Genoa, the cook from Piacenza, Sr. A. Elisabetta and you. Two postulants are to come to you from Ovada and will go to S. P. d'Arena; so from that house you could take Sr. A. Giacinta at once, and the wardrobe keeper Sr. A. Chiara too, whom you could make nurse;3 Sr. A. Angiola

could do the accounts now and then, for in rough copy you are too good yourself, so you don't need a clerk; so you see, you're 6. Take one, the seventh, from Genoa or Piacenza. You'll see that all will go well.4

4. Stick to what I write and you'll see it will be good. I'd like you to go to Piacenza soon to send me Sr. A. Sofia and Sr. A. Ignazia; try to bring with you the man to slaughter the pigs, as I'd feel easier.5

5. Poss is making proposals I cannot accept; it's impossible. He wants to arrange with the Province to have 60 girls, and that is impossible.6

6. You'll see when you return. I hear he has 70 beds ready, and you can take the Genoa girls there; the others are from Bramaiano; as soon as you arrive and see that Poss's beds are in order, write to the Parish Priest to bring them at once.7 Know that these girls will have only their linen. They won't have the F. 100 like the others, so you can use their linen for the others and make pillowcases from the cloth they have. And whatever the postulants have that is shabby, pass on to the girls; understood? I hope all will go well. Goodbye; I'm tired of writing; I'm without Sr. A. Vincenza,9 your affectionate

M. R.

1 She is bringing order into the Sampierdarena house. Cf. L 183,5; 187,1-2;

189,2.

2 L 188,2. Do not move Sr. A. Elvira Persiani; it is not advisable.

3 She repeats, with some variations, what she had written (cf. L 187,7) about

the Sisters for the new community. Seven were needed, as had been agreed with

the administration, to cover the various duties in the hospital, and she was trying to find

suitable and capable ones.

4 Sr. A. Angiola Degrossi could help her occasionally, because in

rough copy you are too good: you are quite capable of keeping the accounts in rough

yourself, so you don't need a clerk. You'll see that all will go

well: the conclusion is a reassuring encouragement in the face of the considerable difficul-

ties of a new community to which the smooth running of the new hospital was

to a large extent entrusted.

5 Cf. L 189,1 and 2.

6 In a letter of 5.2.1874 Emilio Poss had put a plan to her:

to ask the Province for 100 girls as workers, provided by it with a bed and uniform

outfit, and entrust them to the moral responsibility of the Sisters (cf. letter of Emilio

Poss AFSA, FPof, 74-2), in addition to the 60 girls the Mother was putting forward to him for

r

employment. The Mother rightly considers the proposal unacceptable, as it would burden the Sisters morally with girls of whom she could have no references.

7 The girls from Genoa... from Bramaiano (Bettola - PC). Write to the Parish Priest

Don Matteo Solari to bring them at once.

8 The Bramaiano girls have only their linen; she is therefore to proceed as

the Mother explains.

9 Sr. A. Vincenza was unwell. Cf. L 192,2.

She receives no letters from her, perhaps because she expects a visit soon. The Mother cannot be with her until early June. She recommends prayer.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line this evening, though I'm unwell; perhaps you think I'm coming soon and so you don't write.1 I warn you I shan't be with you until early June.

2. When will the day come that they have everything ready so that I can send the other two?2 I can't wait, for then you'll be able to keep the observance better, won't you?

3. My dear, I urge on you meditation and works of piety, for these are what keep us firm and well grounded in our dear vocation. Without them all is lost; whoever does not pray is damned — that is quite certain.3

Greet all the Sisters for me, and believe me, in haste, yours for ever

affectionate M. R. G.

1 In her reply of 9 February Sr. A. Carlotta apologizes for being slow

to write and repeats her great longing to see her again: "now I have no

consolation left but the thought that I shall be able to embrace you".

2 "Those of the Congregation told me they were pleased." Cf.

L 175,7.

3 The school is going well and the Sisters enjoy the esteem of the authorities and the people.

But the Mother reminds the Superior of the foundation and essence of the apostolate:

prayer and observance.

She advises her how to deal with the postulant teacher who is coming. She wants news of the Piacenza house's finances. She sends two vouchers for reduced railway tickets.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received yours and hear you'll soon go to Piacenza, so I'm addressing this to Piacenza. Dear Francesca, the wickedness of certain people is horrifying.1 Listen: I hear a teacher is to come from Cremona; if on arrival she wants to take the habit at once, you could send her to me with Sr. A. Sofia, and then that teacher would come instead of Sr. A. Ignazia; understand? Sr. A. Sofia and the teacher, the one from Cremona whom you are to clothe; or else send Sr. A. Sofia at once with Sr. A. Ignazia and send the other later. Only it would be good for you to keep her with you, otherwise I'd be afraid.2

2. My dear, I need this one at once, at once; I can't tell you why, it's too serious; my head is truly like a balloon, and besides Sr. A. Vincenza is unwell and in bed; everything is needed for Jesus.3

3. I have so much writing to do that my hand has swollen;4 the worst is that my suffering is worth little, because my vileness is much greater, so everything gets worse; what suffering!

4. I want to know something of Piacenza's temporal affairs. I hope many postulants will enter; if God sent a little providence I'd tell you to pop over here, but how can we now that these tickets have been suspended?5

5. As for those you use, you know that from now on they will need my signature, otherwise they won't be accepted. So I'm sending you two for now; later send me some and I'll sign them; and send me a few manuals, and ask that person to send me the Saint Annes.6

6. For charity's sake, don't take Sr. A. Elvira; leave her where she is, for it would be a muddle; I'd need to talk to you; well, we'll manage by letter. See whether Defilippi would go and give the retreat at S. P. d'Arena, and in Genoa too; it would do great good.7

Goodbye, your affectionate

M. R...

7. If the weather is good, during the two days

you are in Piacenza I'd like the builders to raise the wall of

your room. I commend Poss to you.8 This evening I'll write to you

again. Your affectionate M.

1 Certain people: certainly a Sister; cf. L 185,3.

2 The postulant teacher from Cremona is Zamira Mazzini. She received the religious

habit on 19 March 1874. Sr. A. Sofia and Sr. A. Ignazia, cf. L 188,2 and 4.

3 She would have sent her to replace the Superior she had had to move urgently

from the Trastevere house. Sr. A. Vincenza was there, ill; cf. L 195,1 and 2.

4 My hand has swollen. As Fr Lazaro Marte noted in Fisiono-

mia spirituale di Rosa Gattorno, p. 119, the Mother had the invisible stigmata. Several

times in her letters she mentions what long writing does to her right

hand: swelling or intense pain.

5 The railway discount granted to charitable Institutions

had been suspended.

6 A book entitled ...Manuale delle Figlie di S. Anna quale potrà servire per i

di lei devoti. Piacenza, Tip. Solari, 1869. It had been written by Fr Tornatore.

that person: Fr Tornatore is to send her the pictures of Saint Anne.

7 Sr. A. Elvira, cf. L 190,2. Giuseppe Defilippi, a Vincentian priest, was the

confessor of the two Piacenza communities.

8 Emilio Poss, regarding how the working girls were getting on.

She comforts her, warning her against the enemy who tries to lead to perdition. No, the Mother wants her beside her in Paradise for an eternity of joy, so she must seek God alone and give herself wholly to him. She longs to send two more Sisters to make community life easier.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received your letter; I reply at once to comfort you in your afflictions. My dear, be of good heart, for the devil is the enemy of our good works; he would like to turn us aside so that we might then give in to his desires, which are for perdition, and take us with him to an eternity of pain. No! No! my Carlotta must be with me in Paradise for an eternity of joy, never to be parted again; always close, loving our good, Jesus.1

2. Daughter, learn to love dear God and give him alone all your affections; everything to him; live for him; love him alone.2

3. "O love of my Good, when shall I see my daughter on fire with your love? She is spending her life and is ready to give all her blood for you; so give her the strength and love to be consumed!"3

4. Forward and courage. I note what you say about the Sisters; try to get two beds given you and I'll do the rest, so I can send you the two Sisters sooner; I long to, for then you'll be able to live community life. I fear that being so few you can't.4

5. I hear of your ailment too; I hope you'll reply that you're better and happy. Give these two lines to Sr. A. Adelaide.5

God bless you and the others, and believe me your affectionate

M. R. Have prayers said.

1 The devil... pain. In her letter of 9.2.74 the Sister told her candidly:

"...especially in these days of carnival I feel the temptations more, they are

stronger, the devil puts all sorts of things into my head". Recalling the sound teach-

ing of the Church (cf. 1 Pet 5:8-9), the Mother warns her and with motherly affection

holds her close; she wants her with her, "always close", for an eternity of joy.

2 There is only one remedy: to respond to Love, the one vocation, giving God

her whole self (Deut 6:5).

3 She accompanies her teaching to her daughter by entrusting her to God with an outpouring

of love and determination.

4 The two additional Sisters are expected. Cf. L 191, n. 2; 175,7.

5 It was homesickness for her beloved M. Rosa. Sr. A. Adelaide Cervini, the

teacher.

She is very busy and unwell. She is glad of the good news about her health. She advises her to keep the accounts herself and how to assign the Sisters to the most suitable places and duties. She will send a trunk with furnishings for two Chapels: Sampierdarena and Piacenza (Poss factory). She is to have prayers said to Rosa for the new hospital community.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Although it is recreation time, I am writing because I have no other time; you surely can't imagine how many and what kind of occupations I have; God alone knows. Sr. A. Vincenza is in Trastevere, and besides she has been ill for 8 days; today she got up a little and with her usual whimpering she makes my blood rot; just when I need her, she's always like this.

2. My dear, (I) my pain has also come back stronger than usual, so I'll soon have to apply blisters, for I'm very afraid. I'm in pain, and not a little; what do you expect, seeing myself betrayed on every side, so that I'm not even safe to look around. What suffering! One day you'll hear it all in person; now I don't want to lose myself in these trifles.1

3. Hearing you are well was a great consolation to me; you see, my blessed daughter, amid so many sad things the good God sends us something to console us.

4. Now to what you ask. As for the registers, I tell you that you must do everything, (che) you'll see you'll manage well: recording, rendering accounts; you're enough on your own, for if you pay a little atten-

tion when writing, it's more than good enough, and when you don't know something there's the dictionary.

5. As for the teacher, you can take her with you to Sampierdarena and she'll make her noviciate there. I want a mistress to be appointed, and Sr. A. Concetta can do it. I warn you I may need this one; anyway, for now take her with you, so I'm easy about the postulancy.2 Otherwise in Piacenza I'm always afraid. The one you mentioned is fine too, so don't leave her in Piacenza, and likewise any others you think fit.3

6. I hope Giovanna won't spoil anything in that house. It would be good to remove Apollonia and have her under your eye; at least, you know, she couldn't do so much harm; and I'm glad you're taking Sr. A. Chiara as nurse, so she leaves that house, for she is certainly a religious who needs to be under the whip; and you could take Manuela to get her away from up there. What do you think? For nurses anyone will do. Understood? But I always leave you free to do as you think best; I approve everything; rest easy, my dear, I assure you I'm content.4

7. You'll receive Carlotta's trunk containing the candlesticks — 6 large and 2 small — for Mass, and the altar cards (have them cleaned), the missal, the stand, the crucifix (which also needs cleaning), and a chasuble that can be used for all colours, being gold, for every day except [excluding] the black days; you'll see an unpicked sky-blue dress: have it dyed half purple and half red for two chasubles for your hospital chapel.5 For Poss I already have the chalice and pyx;6 for S. P. d'Arena I'll try to get the chalice, pyx and chasubles, i.e. the white, the green and the black; this dress will serve for two; the Vernengos will make them; I'll send the linen for both, Poss and S. P. d'Arena. Now I'll see about getting the candlesticks too. So you can tell him: the linen, chalice, chasubles, pyx, missal, and, I hope, as I say, the candlesticks.7

8. I'm glad you can put the linen into the wardrobes; that pleases me; I'm only sorry about the pigs. Write to Don Accinelli to send him to you; meanwhile leave everything in order.8

9. You were quite right to think of taking the girl from Bramaiano with you.9 Listen: if they say Don Accinelli should be called to Cortemaggiore for the contract, tell that person I'll send him the power of attorney; there's no need to trouble Accinelli.10

10. I commend to you the Our Father, Hail Mary and Glory Be to my Rosa, said in common. Do you know? It was she who got us the hospital, and if they don't forget this O.H.G. the hospital will flourish — I mean in the hospital, only in the community (of) of that hospital.11 The religious arrived very well; let us bless the Lord for it. For now don't send that person for a change of air (for now); later.12 I think by now you'll know, and I can imagine how you felt on hearing of that unfortunate woman I sent on a journey; ah, dear daughter, how great human malice is!13 If you thought of exchanging Sr. A. Emanuela with someone from Genoa, putting her in Genoa and taking the refectorian, who is very good, I'd do it like this: (essa) send Sr. A. Emanuela to Genoa and take the refectorian. All right, you're content.14 I am your affectionate...

I think I've answered everything. Yours for ever, affectionate

M. R.

1 She calls the daily tribulations trifles, minor and passing, and

does not want to dwell on them; she has more important things to deal with.

2 Regarding the teacher (cf. L 192, n. 2): she will make the postulancy (not the novi-

ciate, as she wrote by mistake), and the mistress of postulants can be Sr. A.

Concetta Vernengo. Perhaps I'll need this one, i.e. the postulant.

3 the one you mentioned: a postulant from Bramaiano (see par. 9) and other

religious as you see fit.

4 Giovanna Bixio will not harm the good running of the house. It

would be good for Sr. A. Apollonia Marchetti to leave and for her to take as nurse

for the hospital Sr. A. Chiara, removing her from the Sampierdarena house, and

also Sr. A. Emanuela.

5 You'll receive the trunk: she is sending the furnishings for the hospital Chapel; the

sky-blue dress can be used to make two chasubles.

6 For the chapel of the Poss factory.

7 She can tell Emilio Poss what has been prepared for the chapel.

8 put in the wardrobe: keep the washed and ironed linen in

the wardrobe. She had still not managed to have the pigs slaughtered. (L 188, n. 3).

9 For signing the Cortemaggiore hospital contract she could

delegate Fr Tornatore.

10 Cf. L. 2, n. 4.

11 Cf. L 186,5. the hospital will flourish, i.e. the community serving the hospital.

12 The religious: Sr. A. Sofia and Sr. A. Ignazia. It is not clear what she

means regarding Fr Tornatore.

13 That unfortunate woman: Sr. A. del S. Cuore Cocchella, whom she had had to remove

from the Trastevere house (cf. L 199, n. 4).

14 Cf. above, par. 6.

Sr. A. Sofia will arrive and later the Mother too will come to see her. She is to take care of herself and console her by getting completely well.

A.M.F.

My Vincenza,

1. Cheer up, for I'm well and on my feet; I tell you that tomorrow morning Sr. A. Sofia will finally go there and come to you at once; tell her for charity's sake not to tell anyone that she is recent, I mean recently clothed;2 I'll come later; meanwhile they'll have breakfast.

2. Get up early and stay in your room; meanwhile this evening try to get the blister to dry by putting cotton wool on it. I hope the things have arrived. Have Sr. A. Cherubina treated at once, for charity's sake, with a mustard plaster.3

3. So get up and try not to leave your room, and meanwhile put all the accounts in order. For charity's sake, take care, for I'd be very sorry if you had a relapse.4 Hearing you're better was an immense consolation to me. So it's up to you to want to console me. Everything in person tomorrow. Your affectionate

M. R.

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 Sr. A. Sofia Pasti, the new Superior (cf. L 188, 2 and 4), only recently

clothed: on 27.12.1873.

3 Sr. A. Cherubina Bartoli was unwell.

4 have a relapse: get worse.

She suggests she guide the new Superior, starting her in the office with suitable advice. Meanwhile she is to try to recover her health fully.

A.M.F.

My beloved daughter,

1. See how the good [God] brings everything to light; yes, the rest will soon be known; meanwhile they'll be talked about everywhere; what boldness these two have! yes, the Holy Mother will punish them well, well.2

2. Try to tell that Superior, Sr. A. Sofia, to be gentle with the Sisters and all heart and kindness, because the Sisters are religious equal to her, and we are all equal. For charity's sake, see that she doesn't bully them but treats them with charity and love.3

3. Take care of yourself, for you'll soon have work to do;4 and see: while you are recovering, try to instruct the Superior, so that she can manage alone, and you'll be able to come here during the day — not every day, but some of them — and we'll be together.5 Today I'm very breathless; enough, let us hope in the Lord.

Goodbye, your

affectionate MADRE ROSA

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 brings everything to light... talked about everywhere. She alludes to the unpleasant

incident at the Trastevere house, of which she gives no details. Meanwhile

news of the two Sisters will spread. One of them, the Superior Cocchella,

had left the Institute.

3 Wise advice that well outlines the character and task of the Superior

in the community.

4 you'll have work to do: she was thinking of sending her to the Mother House, where her

presence was needed, since Sr. A. Francesca had left to be Superior of the

new community of the Sampierdarena hospital.

5 while you are regaining your strength... you can come for a few hours almost

every day and we'll be together.

-

She approves all she has done. She feels very ill; she is to pray God not to take away her suffering but to let her work. She wants to know whether there is any basis for what she has heard about a mortgage Don Accinelli would like to put on the Sampierdarena House, and whether the Piacenza House's debts have been paid or how much remains.

My daughter,

1. I've just received a long letter from you, which I read with great pleasure. I note what you have done and approve everything, and I'm very pleased with how you are acting; I bless God for enlightening you so well.1 For charity's sake, they are not to go to Poss until it is dry; it is true I made the contract that whenever the girls fall ill I'll take them into the big house of Saint Anne, but never that they should go somewhere they might catch illness.2 So you did very well there. Carry on, my dear, and God will bless you.

2. How did you leave word for them to put away the washing? especially the guest-quarters linen, in some room, didn't you? And you'll have left it locked as last time, won't you?3

3. How glad I am that the postulants are good; we need it.

4. For the Chapel linen you can take it from S. P. d'Arena for the ceremony; then for every day you can use what I sent you.

5. I hear the little room is in such disorder; listen, what are they going there for? I don't want anyone writing there except you and the Father;

what a business! you should have locked it, then they wouldn't have gone scribbling there any more.5

6. My dear, what can I say, this evening [my head] is spinning so much that I don't know what (mi) I'm writing.

7. Listen, find out what it means that I hear Accinelli — so they say, though I don't believe it — wants to put a mortgage on the S. P. d'Arena house; if you knew how they abused me, as if I were squandering the [patrimony of] all my children! Don't say anything, for charity's sake, to D. Accinelli.6

8. Alas! I'm breathless again; have a novena made for me so that, if it please God, I may work; let him not take away my suffering, but let me work if it please him.7 As for that Sister, I hope I have done everything, and my God granted me the grace that all has been restored to peace. What a consolation! Thank God for it.8 You tell me nothing about what remains to be paid in Piacenza. If you could have asked the municipality for the rest, what do you think?9 Enough, you have done everything well, and I tell you that you are my consolation amid so many troubles. What can I do, my dear: you tell me not to write in my own hand; what can I do? sometimes I have no one to whom [...].

9. I commend Alessandro to you; see how he is getting on; persuade him to stay with Don Accinelli and rely on him in everything, and he'll see he'll be content, and God will soon console him. Let him be sure I always think of him and suffer a great deal for him, my God! My Francesca, I commend him to you; look after him and write me something;10 and about the debts of that house you know of, whether they are paid or a lot is still needed to pay them all, and whether that person has taken the chemist's bills to the Marchioness.11

Goodbye, yours for ever

MADRE [ROSA]

1 In her letter of the same day Sr. A. Francesca tells her everything

she has done in the house, from the washing to everything else.

2 They are not to go to Poss until it is dry. Sr. A. Francesca had gone to the

factory to see how the accommodation of the working girls was

arranged and had found that the dormitories were damp, freshly

whitewashed and very cold, and the girls, and the Sisters too, could fall

ill. So she had spoken to the doctor about it.

3 She had kept the linen in the cupboard and locked it.

4 For the hospital chapel linen, you can use that of the

Sampierdarena chapel for the inauguration ceremony.

5 There was, Francesca had written, great disorder in the Mother's

study. She should lock it; there was no need for them to go there to write.

6 She has heard talk of the mortgage, but it is clearly an unfounded

rumour.

7 The Mother feels ill and, gripped by breathlessness, asks her daughter

for prayers for her health. Then she resumes other topics.

8 That Sister. Cf. L 192 n. 3 and 196,1.

9 The debts never fully paid off were a perennial problem. Sr.

A. Francesca replied that a total debt of

L. 1,880 remained to be paid (cf. letter of 20.2.74).

10 Cf. L 187,5. Alessandro, no longer at school, worried her greatly.

11 She returns to the problem raised in par. 8 (note 9). She wants exact

figures on the Piacenza House's finances and to know whether Fr Tornatore has

handed the Chemist's bill to Marchioness Fanny Anguissola.

She is to keep Sr. A. Teresa ready, as the Mother wants to make her a Superior. She is to keep the novice at Sestri. The Mother awaits news of the Sisters' move to the Sampierdarena hospital. She is to go in good time to the Archbishop for his blessing. The Mother is worried about the Piacenza house. She is to look after Alessandro.

A.M.F. My daughter,

1. Today I had a bad headache and couldn't write as I meant to, for I'm anxious, having no letters from you. The last I had on Tuesday; today is Saturday and I have none.1 Listen: I'd like you to do something for me with all your skill and prudence: find a tactful way to withdraw Sr. A. Teresa and keep her ready for me, as I need her to put in a house as Superior. Silence.2

2. I'm now writing to Insani about the contract and will send the power of attorney to Sr. A. Tomasina, only for signing, because I don't want the one you know of to.3

3. For charity's sake don't send the teacher you (tu) [ti] took with you, even if you clothe her; first see that in that house at Sestri there is a bed furnished with a mattress and what is needed, for I'd be sorry if she could write anything [against us].4

4. Tell me, what will that Sr. A. Guarina do!, who I gather from your letter is at the big house? For charity's sake, if only she could be brought to Genoa or S. P. d'Arena, where you are nearby, for she makes me so afraid with that vice-superior. What do you say?5

5. Listen: have you received a letter of mine addressed to S. P. d'Arena? I can't wait to be able to put "Hospital" on them, so they'll reach you much better, and to hear that you've made the contract.6 For charity's sake don't forget to go to the Archbishop for his blessing and let him know you are the Superior of the Hospital — this only for the good of the poor Institute, which badly needs it.7

6. My dear, I urge something else on you: don't sign any more travel tickets, because they have forbidden it, and if it happened we'd risk losing the concession.8 Tell the others; meanwhile I'll enclose one each time I write, so you'll come to have a good supply.

7. Listen, my dear: Sr. A. Sofia is good for nothing, not even... My God! I don't know where my head is; she is good only for being with the P...9 Anyway, see whether among the religious you have in Genoa or elsewhere a good one comes to mind.10

8. How horrible! This time I don't know what to think; one thing grieves me greatly: knowing those two are at Piacenza, Sr. A. Giovanna and Sr. A. Geronima; you can't believe it.11

9. Listen: Alessandro writes today that he wants the money. Do me the kindness of saying something to him. How this boy distresses me, what sorrow! What he does with it I cannot understand. I hope you'll be a mother to him; don't protect him so much, but correct him and then write and tell me something.12

Goodbye, yours for ever,

affectionate M.

1 Today is Saturday, 21 February.

2 Sr. A. Teresa was in the Genoa house. Silence: it was premature to speak of it.

3 She is writing to Canon Stefano Insani about the contract; she will send the power of attorney to

Sr. A. Tommasina Viterbo to sign; she does not want anyone else

to do it: cf. L 194,9.

4 The teacher you took with you: Zemira Mazzini. Cf. L 192, n. 2.

5 She asks whether it would be wise to move a Sister to Sampierdarena,

so that she can guide her, since the Vice-Superior of the Mother House does not

seem capable to her.

6 put "hospital": address them to the hospital. The Sisters had not yet

settled there. The contract with the administration had not been concluded.

7 The Archbishop, Mgr Salvatore Magnasco, as the correspondence

shows, was not favourable to the FSA.

8 The travel tickets: the vouchers for the railway reduction granted

to charitable Institutions. The Superior General's signature was required.

9 Sr. A. Sofia Pasti, whom she wanted to make Superior (cf. L

195,1; 196,2), was unsuitable; good only for being with the P.: stopping to talk with

the Priests.

10 Try to find me a suitable religious.

11 She is distressed to know that these two Sisters, who

were not exemplary, are in the Piacenza house.

12 Cf. L 187,5; 189, n. 4; 197,9.

She answers various questions on how to organize the Sisters' service at the hospital and on the advisability of preferring certain Sisters. Sr. A. Vincenza will go to Piacenza to sign the Cortemaggiore contract. The Mother will be left alone in Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm answering your letter at once. You tell me what you think about the portress; she seems too young to me, but you'll see better; it would be better to put an old one there, and she should always open the door — not sometimes the man and sometimes the nun; always the nun.2 For the rounds, it's good that you always go in twos; if they can be combined, you could go with the male nurse, as you must always withdraw in twos. With the doctor, provided he keeps his distance from you, you'll always go in twos. Do as that person told you.3

2. Your fear of being a traitor is a real temptation, and I want you instead to answer it: you show yourselves to be beings who never did well...4

3. My dear, how right is the point of our Rules never to be alone! For pity's sake never fail in this; you'll be glad of it. You must know that this flighty one trampled that point underfoot; I can't understand how these ones came to know; who can have told them?5

4. What will Sr. A. Giovannina do in the S. P. d'Arena house if she is no longer in the kitchen? For charity's sake send her to Genoa, where they'll need her badly. For the rest, I hope you've received two letters of mine already and will get Sr. A. Teresa ready for me;6 as for the rest, [Sr.

A. del] Redentore is very good, but Stanislaa — be careful — is very dangerous for the hospital. You'll have to keep an eye on her. What will Angiola do? She can be wardrobe keeper; Sr. A. Apollonia had better stay with you, for it would be a bad business if she went to the house.7 As regards Don Accinelli, you did very well. Oh, how I'd have liked this Sister to go to the hospital as portress; she's strong, old and plain.8

5. If this reaches you in time, I'd be inclined to wait two more days before the girls go to Piacenza; Sr. A. Vincenza will be there on the 4th or 5th of the month; she is going to sign the contract with Cortemaggiore. Meanwhile she will stop for Poss and take a look at the house, for I'm anxious.9

6. In short, my poor little head doesn't know where to rest. Alas! it is a Vesuvius of torments; tribulations pour down on my head in torrents. When I can see you, you'll hear. Imagine, now Sr. A. Vincenza is leaving and I'm left alone, with no one to say a word to; I must keep everything inside my breast; if it doesn't burst, it's a miracle.

7. I keep receiving letters from Alessandro that distress me a great deal; now one thing, now another. Imagine, now he asks me for my power of attorney; what do you think? Alas, I can't move from here.10

8. I await your reply to the two letters I addressed to you at S. P. d'Arena. Write and tell me whether you got them; I'm worried they may have gone astray. Greet everyone for me; your affectionate for ever

MADRE [ROSA]

1 The date is inferred from the context, from the arrival date on the postmark

on the envelope and, in particular, from the date of the letter the Mother is answering:

20.2.1874.

2 about the portress: Sr. A. Francesca proposes Sr. A. Candida Carboneschi,

but the Mother does not seem entirely in agreement; she thinks her too young for the

post (she is 27) and also thinks it better that the Sister alone should be

responsible for the door and not alternate with a male nurse

as the President proposed.

3 To accompany the doctor on the daily round, you should always

be two. Do as Fr Tornatore advised.

4 "Since you wrote to me about those Sisters," writes Sr. A. Francesca, "I am

afraid... I tell the Lord that sooner than I should transgress and betray you, may he

let me die at once. Here they know that S. Cuore is no longer with us." The Mother

answers in kind, so as to reassure her; she tells her how to speak to this

flighty one who was in Genoa. Through these words of Sr. A. Francesca, who

openly names Sr. A. del S. Cuore Cocchella, whereas the Mother has always

refrained from doing so, we learn who the unfortunate woman was whom she had had to move from the Trastevere House in Rome (cf. L 194, n. 13; 196,1; 197,8).

5 The consequence of the reflections and warnings above: it is essential

to observe the point of the Rules that this flighty one trampled on.

6 I hope you have already received: L 197 and 198, and that you'll have Sr.

A. Teresa ready for me.

7 As for the rest: regarding the Sisters you mention next. The Mother makes her

own observations and gives pertinent advice.

8 Regarding Don Accinelli. Sr. A. Giacinta Antoniazzi had asked Sr.

A. Francesca whether she could speak to Don Accinelli about the problems of the

Sampierdarena house. Sr. A. Francesca had advised her to be prudent. Oh,

how I'd have liked it!: this is the Sister the Mother thought suitable as

portress. She was 39 and had received the religious habit in January

1872.

9 If this letter reaches you before the departure of the 8 girls from Sam-

pierdarena who are to work in the Poss factory, try to make them wait

two more days so that they find Sr. A. Vincenza there on arrival.

10 Cf. L 198,9.

To the Sister, distressed at receiving a sad letter from her sister Sr. A. Augusta, she recommends peace and that she write giving her suitable advice.

My daughter,

1. I'm replying post-haste to relieve your distress.1 Listen: answer Sr. A. Augusta at once and tell her she is a real little madcap, for I can't understand how she could write such a thing to you when she has comforting letters from me; and if she was wrong, it means that when she submits in obedience not to do it again, the Lord is so good that he forgives.2 See, my dear daughter, tell her also never again to write to you in such terms that upset you, and not to be upset herself, for you know her character: she is upset by little things; and even if it were a big thing, we are not infallible, but wretched human creatures who, if the good God did not uphold us with his right hand, would sink into the abyss of our iniquities.3

2. Cheer up, for charity's sake, don't be upset, for I know how much harm such things do; anyway, my dear daughter, you did well to write to me at once like this; the fountain can give you the water of peace.4

Goodbye, for I'm posting it at once. Yours for ever,

Affectionate M. R.

1 The Sister wrote to her on 21.2 about her sister: "this evening I was struck by some bad news... Sr. A. Augusta is so distressed about something that has happened to her, but she doesn't tell me what it is. She begs me to inter-

cede with you and tell you to do anything to her, but not to stop her being a Daughter of Saint Anne".

2 The Mother plays it down: tell her she is a real little madcap. What had hap-

pened? Sr. A. Francesca Camisa, on going to Sampierdarena, had pointed out to her

some negative aspect of how she governed the community. Cf. L 187,

1-2. The Mother had treated her lovingly: she has comforting letters from me.

3 See, my dear daughter. With kindness and calm she clarifies aspects

of the Sister's character: she is upset by little things; and even if it were a serious

matter, she must remember that we are not infallible...

4 Cheer up... peace. The conclusion is superb: a pearl of educational,

spiritual and highly poetic value.

She asks her to send medicines. She is pleased with the Sisters' good dispositions; they are to pray for her intentions. She appreciated their letter. She urges her to keep Alessandro's clothes in order and explains how to handle requests for reduced rail fares.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line, as I'm very busy and in poor health. I'm on my feet thanks to Signora Maddalena's decoction,1 but unfortunately I have none left and my breathlessness has come back. My dear, see whether you can get a little just for me. At least Carlotta is well and no longer vomiting. So do me this kindness and add some chocolate and orange-flower water, as soon as you can.

2. Your letters console me as I hear what the Lord deigns to do in his poor daughters. I long to hear soon that you have a big house;2 I want you to ask the Sisters for me to say privately three Our Fathers, Hail Marys and Glory Bes to the Sacred Heart of Jesus for my intention.

3. Please see to Alessandro's clothes; I'd like you to fetch them all from Mamma's house and mend and iron them for him;3 tell him it was I who told you to; tell him first, so you'll be in agreement and do everything prudently.

4. I'm pleased about the providence too. Oh, how I

bless the Lord for it! and amid my countless labours I am always with you.

5. Greet all the Sisters for me and thank them for the letter

they wrote me; tell them I'm not answering because I haven't

time, but that I appreciated it very much; meanwhile I bless them, as every

day I hold them close in the Heart of Jesus, that he may make them a furnace

of love; let them pray, for I need it so much. Yes, by all means increase

the little purse; I'm happy for you to.4 Goodbye, my daughter. The Lord

bless you, and believe me always your

Affectionate M. ROSA

6. P.S. Give this note to the Superior Sr. A.

Francesca. The ones you have are no longer any use, because

they must first be signed by me, otherwise the concession could be

suspended and they won't be accepted; for charity's sake, don't sign any more.5

1 The decoction was prepared by Signora Maddalena Bacigalupo.

2 You have a big house. The one they live in is now too small for the number

of Sisters, and enlarging it was being considered. (Cf. letter of Accinelli to Sup. Francesca

14.3.1874).

3 Alessandro's clothes... I'd like you to mend and iron them (so-

prassassi).

4 the little purse: the small nest egg of savings.

5 Cf. L 198,6.

She wants her to find a new confessor for the two Sampierdarena communities. She urges her to watch over the other house and entrusts Alessandro to her. Her tribulations are many and grave. She awaits news of the Hospital contract.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm answering by return of post the letter I've just received. I note what you say about the confessor; I tell you I'm not very happy with him either and would like you to find another for both houses, for yours and for our house; you could go to the Curia and to the Archbishop himself — he is obliged to find one; let him know you'd like a Jesuit or a missionary.2

2. I'm glad to hear the teacher is doing well; what will be done for Sestri? Let's hope the Lord sends another; I was so worried. If Don Accinelli had taken a qualified teacher from Genoa — alas! it would have been a real muddle.3

3. I urge you to watch over the house and go there now and then; perhaps now that all the ringleaders have been removed it will go better; and stand firm that the new ones drop the habit of chattering with outsiders, such as the P...4

4. I'm very pleased with what you wrote me about Piacenza.5 Tell the postman always to bring your letters to the hospital, and at the end of the year you'll give him something; so you'll get them sooner; I'll address them to the hospital, and there'll be no mix-ups.

5. If that young Genoese girl could qualify for the diploma, it would be a fine thing.

6. For charity's sake keep an eye on Alessandro; I commend him to you; be a mother to him.6 I hear he's beginning to run up small debts; for charity's sake advise him to get rid of this ugly habit; I've written to him that I'll never pay them and he'd better think about it. What has he done with it? He tells me no one looks after his clothes; see that the nuns mend them; let them go to the house and fetch them; it's an excuse, for he tells me that this way he buys new ones. What a business! If you knew how he strangles me with his letters.

7. My dear Francesca, the tribulations weighing on my head these months are so many that I can't bear it; last night I thought I would die; I had such a violent convulsion, from the very weakness of thinking: here there are big troubles, down there the same; I see myself without strength, barely able to stand; I don't know what to think of doing first.

8. I hope soon to receive a letter saying that you have opened and made the contract.

9. See about the lawsuit; if you need to go and commend yourselves, speak to Don Accinelli.

Goodbye, your affectionate for ever

M. R.

1 The date is inferred from the context. The Mother is answering a letter of Sr.

A. Francesca of 20.2.74.

2 what you say about the confessor. "You can see he is one of those with little

experience, he's eccentric, says the Superior Augusta," she wrote verbatim.

3 The teacher is a postulant. But there is still no teacher for Sestri Ponente.

Fortunately Don Accinelli had not engaged a lay teacher from Genoa.

4 ...watch over the Sampierdarena house; with the ringleaders — the Sisters

of "little religious spirit" — removed, it will go better. Chattering with people outside the

community, with the Priests.

5 She had put everything in order at home and spoken with Emilio Poss about

the factory girls.

6 Poor Alessandro and poor mother! But there is one who for love of both

becomes a Mother: good Francesca. Cf. L 198,9 and n. 12; 199,7.

She asks for the faculty to have the Holy Week services celebrated in the communities.

Most Holy Father,

1. The Mother Superior of the Daughters of Saint Anne, Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno, prostrate at the feet of Your Holiness, begs the favour of being able to hold all the Holy Week services in all her houses where there are no fewer than twelve Religious,2 and, besides the Mass of Christmas night granted her by Your Holiness, to have the other two celebrated.

2. This she hopes for, and will receive the favour as from Heaven.

[Sister ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne]

1 The date is taken from the grant, at the foot of which is written: ex auden-

tia SS.mi die 26 februarii 1874.

2 Easter fell that year on 5 April.

Marchioness Carrega has decided to take the habit of the Daughters of Saint Anne and is preparing. She asks his blessing, to give her strength and consolation.

Most Reverend Eminence,

1. I would have come (in) earlier to ask you what I am about to tell you in writing, if my poor health these days, worse than usual, did not make me unable to go out.

2. A month ago Marchioness Carrega decided to take the habit of Saint Anne, and has already received the blessing at the Holy Father's feet.2 Now, before this act takes place, which will be in a month, I should like Your Eminence to bless this dear daughter, that it may give her strength and consolation in the retreat she is making.3

3. God alone gives this, through his Apostles and those who holily bear the far from light burden of the pastoral [ministry].

4. Full of confidence and relying on your immense charity, we await a word together with the blessing, while, prostrate as the least of your flock, we kiss your sacred right hand, and full of veneration I remain your

Most humble Daughter Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO

1 The autograph draft omits the addressee and date. They are inferred from the

context.

2 She was received with the Mother on 1 February 74; cf. L 186,2.

3 The clothing, set for 25 March, was later postponed to 19 April.

Cf. 220,3.

She has heard that the Ladies of the Circle fear she will ask to be reimbursed for the meals given to the pupils. She states that it never occurred to her to charge them and declares that if the Sisters' entirely disinterested work is met with distrust, she is ready to withdraw them from the school.

Most Illustrious Madam President,

1. Following many guarded questions that the Lady Visitors of the school2 asked about the soup which, thank God, is distributed daily to these needy little ones, I have come to learn that your Ladyships fear I may now compel the Circle to reimburse me for the expenses incurred for this purpose.

2. No, I have no such intention; indeed the thought of charging this Most Respectable Circle with the cost of this work never even crossed my mind. But be assured, Most Illustrious Ladies, that if I presented the Circle with a statement of income and expenditure, it was in response to the very many pressing requests of your Ladyships, who wished to know where all the [expenses] came from.

3. As for the claim that I received from the most worthy Parish Priests the L. 75 that previously went to this Most Honourable Circle, I candidly declare it is not true. I received only L. 15 from the Parish Priest of S. Angelo.3

4. What greatly pains and grieves me is to see our work,4 entirely disinterested in every respect, met with such distrust.

5. I consider it my duty, however, to inform your Ladyships that if we are a nuisance and a burden to you, I am quite ready to suspend the school.

Please forgive this letter, but I felt obliged to write it to remove all doubt. Accept the sentiments of esteem and respect of one who is honoured to remain

Most humble Obedient ROSA GATTORNO

1 The draft lacks the addressee, but since until 27 May 1874 the

President of the S. Monica Catholic Circle was Princess Bice Altieri, it is

presumed to be addressed to her. There is no firm evidence for the date; it may be from

February-March 1874.

2 The Ladies of the "S. Monica Circle".

3 The Parish Priests. The "S. Monica Circle" extended its work to the benefit of the

parishes of S. Maria in Campitelli, S. Nicola in Carcere, S. Marco and S. Angelo in

Pescheria.

4 our work: from this point to the end the draft is in M. Rosa's hand.

She is still ill. The Mayor has informed her of the opening of the Hospital and the inauguration of the Chapel. She is sending a picture, linen and furnishings for the Chapel. Francesca may take what is needed from the other Sampierdarena house and from the Genoa house. Various advice and errands.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. I haven't written for two days because the breathlessness took hold of me again and I had to apply a blister to be able to breathe; now I breathe better; the blister is still open. What do you expect, my dear: it's the spasms, the anxieties, the constant palpitations that produce this bag of water in me.

2. I'm glad to hear all you tell me about the hospital; I'm only sorry to hear you stay up so late; my dear, it worries me for your health; promise me not to do it again; leave everything.2

3. The Mayor wrote to me; he is delighted; he says that on Sunday the 8th of this month you will open the hospital and the Chapel, and the altar is ready; I'm sending a crate with a picture of the Sacred Heart, linen and an altar cloth, and a chasuble that will serve for all colours; the pyx I'm keeping here with the chalice, as I'm afraid to put it in the crate in case it gets lost; I'll send it at the first opportunity; whatever you lack, take from the house; tell the Mayor that while the things are on their way from here you'll use those of the house; and for the day of the cere-

mony take everything from there, the best things: the gold embroidered chasuble, the fine cope — in short everything, the chalice; in Genoa they have two and can give you one for now, and the monstrance from S. P. d'Arena; for the pyx, get them to give you the small spare one they have at S. P. d'Arena; as for candlesticks, the house could lend you theirs. I want the Municipality not to have to think about anything for the Chapel.3

4. So try to do everything yourself; take from the houses, in my name, whatever you need; I hope you've understood.4 It would be good for the Archbishop to be present at the opening of the Chapel, as I hope the Mayor will have invited him.

5. So put Sr. A. Cecilia at the door, and I'll also write to the Mayor as you say; everything you said the Superior should answer those two vipers is very well said, and the rest too.5

6. Keep going like this, for I'm delighted, and every moment I bless your steps; and remember I'm always with you.

7. Indeed I want you, when you can, to speak to Sr. A. Concetta and tell her you're astonished that a religious should tell untrue things to the postulants; ask her to keep her gossiping tongue in check and get rid of this habit of always speaking ill of the house, for the Lord is weary, and if she doesn't stop it will end badly. Goodbye, yours for ever,

affectionate MADRE

8. P.S. I've just received another of yours and note what you say about the portress; do this: say nothing for now, as there isn't so much work for the moment. We'll talk about it later;6 the lawsuit is Don Ricchini's. If you thought of going to see Advocate Boccardo to find out whether we need to go and commend ourselves to someone.7

9. I hope all will go well. Tomorrow I'm sending the Mayor a fine picture of the Sacred Heart of Jesus; for the opening of the Chapel you can take the large one they have in the S. P. d'Arena chapel. Then you'll send it back. It's good for the Archbishop to come and bless the Chapel. Be of good heart; I like the Archbishop's answer very much; I assure you I'll speak of it at once, and I hope that if they write anything... it really is odd.8 Listen, write a line to the Superior of S. Lazzaro asking him to send you Mr Defilippi for the retreat, both in Genoa and at S. P. d'Arena.9

1 The date is taken from the letters she is answering.

2 You stay up late, "until 11 and midnight, because they want every-

thing in order for the second Sunday of March" (8 March), Sr. A.

Francesca had written on 28.2.

3 ... a chasuble that will serve for all colours: being gold it could be

used for the various feasts requiring particular liturgical colours. Take it

from the house... use those of the house: of the Institute in Sampierdarena.

4 from the houses: of Sampierdarena and Genoa.

5 those two vipers. She repeats the term used by Sr. A. Francesca to

refer to Sr. A. Concetta and Sr. A. Giuseppa Vernengo. They answered the Superior

rudely and made demands about their treatment. Cf. L 82, n. 4; 99, n. 3 and below,

par. 7.

6 She had proposed a portress in addition to the 7 Sisters

agreed, but had also expressed doubt that the Director would think her

necessary.

7 The advocate Domenico Boccardo, Sr. A. Vincenza's uncle, was handling the

case.

8 Sr. A. Francesca had gone to pay her respects to Archbishop Salvatore Ma-

gnasco to inform him of the opening of the Community serving in the hospital and

ask him to assign a confessor. He had answered: "Go to the Missionaries,

and later on...", without specifying anything further.

9 To the Superior of the Alberoni College in Piacenza, to send Fr Giuseppe

Defilippi to preach the Spiritual Exercises to the Genoa and Sampier-

darena communities.

She is pleased with what she wrote about the hospital, approves all she has done and gives her full authority to act as she thinks best. She only obliges her to take care of her health. The Mother is better. She has written to the Mayor about the contract and the Chapel. Francesca is to visit the Sestri house to see how it is going; the Mother has told the Superior.

A.M.F.

My Francesca,

1. I've just received your letter. I note what you say about the hospital and bless God, the author of our good. I'm delighted about the confessor; as for the Vernengo, do as you think best; I give you full authority and will approve whatever you do;2 there is just one thing I cannot approve and shall always oppose: your not taking every care to keep well. Oh, how it consoles me when you tell me you're well! Yes, my dear, try not to overdo things; look after yourself, and then you'll be my consolation.

2. As for Sr. A. Cecilia with Sr. A. Apollonia, yes, call her. Listen, you must know I'm alone at the desk and have to answer all the letters, having sent Sr. A. Vincenza to Piacenza and Ferrara, because... all in person. You want to see me; I want it more than you do.

3. Thanks to the Lord [and] your prayers, the pain has eased a little and I'm breathing better; thank the Sisters for me.

4. You say you'll take the linen from the House, but I wrote to you to take everything needed for the Chapel, for you know I wrote to the Mayor that I'd see to everything.3

5. I have a beautiful pyx and chalice and want to bring you all the rest myself. Listen: when they have held their ceremony, it would be good for you to take the Mayor aside and ask him to let you go and invite the Archbishop to bless the Chapel and the hospital — but only when they have finished their ceremony and you have everything ready in the Chapel.4 You'll see what is best to do. Be sure that as soon as I come down I'll fly to you and we'll be together a good while.

6. I've written to the Mayor and urged him to make the contract, for it is for the good running of things; I hope he'll do it. I also told him I've instructed you to furnish the Chapel and obtain whatever is needed. He's very pleased; this for your guidance.

7. When you've finished your ceremonies I'd like you to go to Sestri to see, for that Superior speaks to me of postulants. Meanwhile you'll hear and write to me how that house is going. I enclose a note for the Superior.5 Goodbye, my dear daughter; I am always and for ever your

affectionate M. R.

8. Tell the Vernengos we have received permission to

hold all the Holy Week services, and tell Don

Accinelli too.6

When you've read it, seal it.7

1 The date is inferred from Sr. A. Francesca's reply of 3 March 1874.

2 About the confessor. "A Jesuit will probably come," Sr. A.

Francesca wrote, "because the Missionaries can't come." As for Sr. A. Concet-

ta Vernengo, do as you think best. Sr. A. Francesca wanted to remove her from

the post of mistress of postulants as unsuitable.

3 Cf. L 206,3,4.

4 When they have held their ceremony: when they have held the civil cere-

mony inaugurating the hospital, ask to invite the Archbishop

to bless the Chapel and the hospital.

5 She wants her to go to Sestri to see how the house is going,

and the postulants, and to deliver to the Superior, Sr. A. Filomena Pugnaloni, the

note enclosed.

6 Tell the Vernengos and Don Accinelli of the permission to hold the Holy Week

services at home. Cf. L 203.

7 She means the note she wrote to the Superior.

She learns from her letter that the Countess's Secretary has gone over the accounts. Clearly outsiders seek their own interest; let it be a rule that a house's problems are to be laid before one's own Superiors for advice and comfort. Now she is to be at peace.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received your letter today and note what you say about the irregularities the Secretary found, for which you naively blame yourself.2 This action, or rather the conduct of outsiders, must serve us as a rule never to trust those who seek nothing but their own (own) interest.

2. Ah, my God, if only the Superiors of Saint Anne would (a)understand once and for all that the affairs of their houses should be known only to the Superiors, and that they must guard all their doings most jealously; see instead what comes of trusting [outsiders]: now everyone everywhere knows what she said; just look.3

3. Whereas when we ask our Superiors for advice and pour out our anguish to them, then indeed all goes well for us and we receive comfort and all the relief we so need.4 Enough, let's leave it all; be at peace, firm and holding fast to your holy Mother Saint Anne. Place every anguish in God, for everything will pass.

Goodbye; greet everyone for me

[MADRE ROSA]

1 The date is inferred from the context.

2 The Secretary of Countess Maria Anna Trotti, Teresina Zagotti, had gone

several times to the Ferrara Institute to check on things and audit the

accounts of the bursar Giuseppe Squarzoni. (Cf. letters of Bucciotti to M. Rosa

February-March 1874).

3 The Superior's fault lay in failing to inform the Mother

of the house's problems. Cf. L 211,1.

4 In the Superiors we find comfort and all the consolations (relief)

we need.

She blesses the Lord who deigns to provide for the community's needs. She thanks her for what she does for Alessandro and for the basket she sent. She hopes Don Accinelli and Alessandro will come to Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received your letter and note how much you gave Don Accinelli in February.1 Blessed be God, who loves us so much, when we deserve to be reproached for our many demerits.

2. Thank you for what you've done for Alessandro, and I approve what you did about the shirts; I received the basket with everything in good condition; thank you very much; may God reward the charity you show this poor Mother of yours.

3. My health is poor, and moreover, having been left alone at the desk for the correspondence, I haven't a minute, and I suffer a great deal from breathlessness.

4. Ask Don Accinelli to tell me what he will do with the things I have at Mamma's house, whether he has thought of keeping or selling them; it's a curiosity that came to me.2

5. Yesterday evening Anna wrote to him asking him to come; tell him so from me; I mean for him to come with Alessandro, and the journey will be entirely at my expense; we'll settle terms beforehand.3

Goodbye, your affectionate. Give my regards to the Sisters, and God bless you all, while I remain

your affectionate M. R.

1 The letter she is answering is missing.

2 The things I have at mamma's house: the furniture left to her

as an inheritance at her father's death; Accinelli, as her attorney, was

dealing with it. Cf. L 189, n. 3.

3 Marchioness Anna Carrega had invited Don Accinelli to attend the

ceremony of her clothing. The Mother invites him too, together with Alessandro.

She has received the letter written from Florence station. She now awaits news of the Piacenza house. She is better. Vincenza is to take care of herself and ask the doctor for something for her cough.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your letter written from Florence; blessed be God who accompanied you so well. Now I'm anxiously awaiting one telling me what you did with that Lady from Bologna.1

2. Write at once and tell me how you found the Piacenza house; I hear other postulants have entered, and you can have a look.

3. My health is much better and I'm no longer so breathless; the decoction is doing me good. For charity's sake take care of yourself; [for] the cough ask Albertazzi what he says and have him prescribe something, so it goes away completely.2

4. Nothing new here; the torments increase instead of decreasing. When you come, don't forget to bring some manuals of Saint Anne.3

Goodbye, so I can send it to the post, your

Affectionate M. R.

1 The Lady from Bologna is the secretary of Countess Maria Anna Trotti.

(Cf. L 208,1; 211,1).

2 Sr. A. Vincenza had been ill (cf. L 194,1) and was left with a cough.

She is to see the community doctor Sante Albertazzi and have him prescribe

some remedy.

3 The manuals: cf. L 192, n. 6.

Her letter gave her great consolation. God helped her in replying. She is to take care of herself: the Mother has no other wish or consolation than to know she is well. She has sent the paper with the permissions for the Holy Week services.

A.M.F.

My dear daughter,

1. Although it's very late, I want to answer your letter, which I received after lunch; I leave you to imagine the consolation I felt: how well you answered her! God was helping you; courage, forward! It was just as I thought: that flighty Superior had confided things to her that she should not have; this is a lesson.1

2. I hope that on your return you found her unchanged; I haven't received anything yet.2

3. For charity's sake look after yourself; you know I have no wish or consolation but to know you're well; you must spare nothing for your health, and you'll always give me great pleasure when you write that you no longer have a cough.3

4. My breathlessness is much better, and the decoction I'm taking — I've already had a bottle and a half — is doing me a lot of good. The pain has greatly eased.

5. Mgr Mariano sends his regards; Mgr Negrotto sent me the permissions paper today with approval for everything, and I've already had two copies made to send one to Piacenza and the other to Genoa; I think the Stradone house won't do anything; it could be used for the factory Chapel, if there are priests.4

I can't wait to receive another letter from you with lots of news.

Goodbye, for it's too late. I am your affectionate for all ages, your

M. R.

Give my regards to that person.

1 Cf. L 210,1 and the relevant note.

2 Perhaps she means the Superior. Sr. A. Vincenza had given her good ad-

vice (cf. letter of 5.3.74 to M. Rosa).

3 For charity's sake look after yourself. Sr. A. Vincenza's health worried her. Cf. L 210,

n. 2.

4 Mgr Mariano Wanstienkist; Mgr Augusto Negrotto. For the approv-

al: cf. L 203.

She asks that the subsidy granted annually by the Municipality for the orphan girls cared for in the Institute be granted for the current year.

Most Illustrious Mayor,

1. Encouraged by your kindness, which I have already experienced many times, I make bold to present this petition, trusting that it will be favourably received.

2. For several years now this honourable Municipality has granted me a subsidy for the poor girls placed in this Institute by the Municipality itself at the time of the last cholera epidemic, and it has always served to clothe them and partly to provide for their other most urgent needs.

3. Now the Superiors of our houses to which I sent these girls — since lack of space prevented my keeping them in this house3 — urge me to take steps to obtain this subsidy again this year, and I turn to Your Most Illustrious Lordship asking you to see that it is granted me.

4. To encourage you to grant what I respectfully ask, I beg you to consider how hard it is for this poor Institute, which lives partly on charity, to maintain, with provisions as dear as they are, girls from whom it can derive very little if any benefit, and to supply all they need; and then, in your immense kindness, to see that the Honourable Municipality grants this petition and allows me a subsidy equal to that granted in past years.

5. For this, as for every other favour, I shall

always be most deeply grateful, as I assure you the gratitude of the girls benefited will be eternal. With perfect esteem I profess myself

[Sr. A. ROSA GATTORNO]

1 He was the acting Mayor at the time.

2 In the register "Elemosine 1866/87", AFSA, under March the sum of

L. 300 is recorded as the annual subsidy from the Municipality. In relation to this date, and

considering that no such entry appears in the same register

in subsequent years, this letter is presumed to belong to this peri-

od. Throughout March the Mother was in Rome. She may have had

this letter sent from Piacenza, as on other occasions. Cf. L 5.

3 She had moved some resident girls from the Mother House to the Institutes of

Sampierdarena and Ferrara.

She asks a "special blessing" for the new Chapel about to open at the Poss factory.

Most Holy Father,

1. I, Sister Anna Rosa Gattorno, Superior of the Daughters of Saint Anne, prostrate at the feet of Your Holiness, beg you to impart a very special Blessing on a new Chapel of ours that will open in a few days at Piacenza in the house of an Austrian non-Catholic.2

2. The premises were built and fitted out as a factory, where there are already 18 Religious, directing and supervising more than 200 poor resident girls and 300 non-resident ones who help in that great silk works.3

3. The said Gentleman, though a Protestant, has already given a very large room for the internal Oratory, which will hold more than 500 people.

4. The decorations, vestments and sacred furnishings for the Altar were all supplied by the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne. All that is lacking, Most Holy Father, is your Blessing, to confirm the work undertaken and be an effective incentive to the conversion and return to the arms of our Church of the said Mr Aless. Poss, an Austrian.

This I hope, that of the grace...

[Sister ANNA MARIA ROSA GATTORNO Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne]

1 This date is presumed from the context. The chapel was inaugurated on 13 April

1874.

2 a new chapel of ours: ours in that she had wanted it for the

Sisters and the working girls lodged at the factory itself of Alessandro Poss,

a Protestant.

3 The premises... silk. Cf. Appendix IV.

She suggests how to deal with the postulants and with a Sister to be moved. She is to go to the Poss factory to see how the girls are. The Mother has at heart the settling of the Piacenza house, which needs a capable Superior. Some advice and errands.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your second letter describing in detail the scene in Bologna. What brainless heads!2 You also tell me you've received the money from the Marquis, 250 F.; that pleased me too.3 Ah, I hope the Eternal Father will send you everything; if so, the house can be strengthened and a good number of postulants taken in.

2. You tell me you are sending the postulant from Bramaiano to S. P. d'Arena. For charity's sake, you'd better clothe her, for I shall need her here; I'd be inclined to clothe her and then take her to replace Elvira; depending on what you tell me, because from the Superior's letter I gather Sr. A. Elvira can't be left there any longer.4 Tell Sr. A. Tomasina I haven't answered her because you would have done everything; so you can take her away and send her to S. P. d'Arena, for I see we shan't come out of it well; indeed, be quick about it.5

3. How many girls are there? Mind that the sick ones, I mean, all go to the Morte, as I told you. Why did Poss make such a fuss? When everything isn't in order yet.6

4. I hope you'll be able to do well; one thing weighs on my heart, and that is

being able to give the house a capable Superior; I'd really like her to reach you before you leave, so you could leave everything in better order.7

5. How is Colomba — is she upset? Did she also have lunch with the Countess?8 How did you find the house — in order?

6. If you find the postulants there are good, it's better to have them make three days' retreat before you leave and then clothe them.

7. My health is fairly good; the breathlessness has stopped. Let's hope it doesn't come back. Yesterday Carlotta wasn't very well; better today, only she has a cough. It's very cold here and the weather is bad.

8. I hope you've given my letters to that person and told him what I asked you to.9

9. Don't bring or send chocolate, for we've found some very good; don't forget the manuals of Saint Anne!10 Tomorrow I hope to receive a letter from you telling me something more detailed about the house; I'm always on tenterhooks, for it matters a great deal to me.

10. If you haven't yet had the chalice repaired, see about

replacing its foot with one of the composite ones; you'll see. Don't

forget to send the duck to Signora Maddalena.11 Tell

that person that in Genoa they are taking the room below that he want-

ed, one of those sisters having died.12

Goodbye, the pen won't write any more. Yours for ever,

Affectionate M. [ROSA]

11. Your mamma has written, but she says nothing that needs a re-

ply, nothing of consequence; so you'll get it when you come,

your affectionate M...

1 The date is taken from the context.

2 Sr. A. Vincenza has told her of Countess Trotti's reception and the

pretences of the lady companion, Signora Ninetta: "Scenes from the theatre" (cf. in-

complete undated letter, 1874).

3 This is Marquis Marsigli of Bologna. He had promised that money to Sr. A.

Sofia Pasti.

4 The postulant from Bramaiano could replace Sr. A. Elvira, because the

Superior Francesca has written that she is unhappy at Sampierdarena.

5 Tell Sr. A. Tommasina Viterbo I haven't written because you would

see to the necessary changes.

6 The sick are to be moved to the infirmary of the House in Via del-

la Morte, better equipped than that of the Mother House. Cf. L 83,4.

7 weighs on my heart: I am anxious to find a capable and suit-

able superior for the Mother House.

8 Colomba Grampini, cf. L 188, n. 5. Sr. A. Vincenza had accompanied her

to Piacenza.

9 to Fr Tornatore.

10 The manuals: cf. L 192, n. 6.

11 ...to Signora Maddalena Bacigalupo; she wanted to repay the favour

she did her in preparing the healing "decoctions".

12 The house was too small for the number of Sisters. Fr Tornatore had pointed

this out. It seems the right opportunity had now come. The adjoining room he had

advised taking had become free on the death of the tenant.

(Cf. letter of Accinelli 27.2.74).

She encloses a letter to be delivered to the Father. She asks for information about a girl working at Poss.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. This is the third time I've written and you haven't yet sent me a letter. Deliver this one of mine to its destination.2 I'm fairly well.

2. I'd like to know how the girl Malfatto3 at Poss is in health and whether she is good, and whether we should accept her sister, whom they're asking me to take; write to me at once, and she'll come with another. Goodbye, yours in haste.

Goodbye. Give my love to Carlottina.

[MADRE ROSA]

1 The date is inferred from the context.
